paragraphs.text: Lesson 31. Asking permission and asking indirect questions.
As you learned in the last lesson, the words you use make a big difference in whether your
phrase is polite or impolite. Today we're going to study examples of how to ask questions
in a polite and indirect way. Conversation. Asking permission. Liz is staying at her friend
Mary's house for a few days. Listen to their conversation. It's getting late. I'm going to bed.
Okay. Would it be alright if I watch TV for a few more minutes?
Sure. Go right ahead. Oh, and also can I use your phone charger? My cell phone battery's
almost dead. No problem. Here you go. I'm leaving for work early tomorrow morning. Feel
free to eat anything you find in the fridge. Thanks. Do you mind if I cook? I might want
to make an omelet or something. Not at all. Just please make sure to clean up afterwards.
I will. By the way, what time are you getting home tomorrow? Probably around six. Why?
Do you think I could have a key so that if I go out, I could get back in before six?
Sorry, but I actually can't give you one. The landlord doesn't let anyone in the building
give out spare keys, you know, because of security concerns. He's pretty strict about it.
Oh, okay. No worries. Good night. Good night. Conversation vocabulary and phrases. Liz uses
several different phrases to ask Mary for permission. Here are various ways to do this
in English. Can I plus a verb? For example, can I borrow your pen? Could I plus a verb?
For example, could I have a little piece of your sandwich? May I plus a verb? For example,
may I take the day off from work tomorrow? Asking for permission with may is now considered
very formal, and most people use one of the other expressions on this list instead. Do
you think I could plus verb? Do you think I could stay at your place over the weekend? Do
you mind if I smoke? Would you mind if I plus verb in the past tense? Would you mind if I
used your computer for a few minutes? Is it okay if I plus verb? Is it okay if I open the
window? Would it be okay or would it be all right if I plus verb in past tense? For example,
would it be all right if I opened the window? Would it be possible for me to plus verb? Would
it be possible for me to call you at home later tonight? The most common phrases in that list
are can I, could I, and is it okay if I? The expressions beginning with would are the most
formal. Notice the form of the verb in each phrase. The questions would you mind if I, and would
it be okay or all right if I? Use the verb in the past tense, even though you are asking permission
for an action in the present or future. Mary says yes to a number of lizzes requests. Here
are some expressions for giving permission in English. Sure. Go ahead. Go right ahead. No
do you mind or would you mind questions? To say no to someone's request in a polite way,
you can use one of these phrases. I'd prefer if you didn't or I'd prefer if you don't.
I'm afraid that's not possible. That's more formal. Sorry but, and then give a reason why
you must say no. That's more informal. Asking indirect questions. Direct questions are the
normal questions beginning with who, what, when, where, why, how, and do, does, or did.
We can use direct questions with friends and colleagues who we know well. Indirect questions
are used when we want to add a little extra politeness, for example, when speaking with
someone we don't know, with the person who we respect or who is in a position of authority,
or when asking a question of a sensitive nature. For example, a direct question is, where is the
bathroom? To ask that question indirectly, you could say, could you tell me where the bathroom
is? Here are some phrases you can use to ask indirect questions. With examples, when asking
for information, you can say, could you tell me? For example, could you tell me how much this
t-shirt costs? Do you know? For example, do you know if there's a bank around here? Do
you have any idea? For example, do you have any idea what time the next bus is coming?
Use the first phrase, could you tell me? When you're asking somebody who probably has the
answer, for example, asking an employee in the store how much the t-shirt costs? Use, do
you know if there's a possibility that the other person doesn't know the answer? And
use, do you have any idea? If there's little possibility that the other person knows the
answer? When asking if something is possible, use these phrases. Would it be possible? For
example, would it be possible for you to finish the project by tomorrow? Is there any
chance? For example, is there any chance that we could reschedule the meeting? Use these
for questions that would normally use can or could in the direct question form. Can you
finish the project by tomorrow? Becomes, would it be possible for you to finish the project
by tomorrow? Could we reschedule the meeting? Becomes, is there any chance that we could reschedule
the meeting? When asking any type of question or favor, you can use these phrases. I was
wondering if you could give me a ride. I'd like to know. I'd like to know what kind of
classes are offered here at the community center. I'd like to know if you have any products
on sale at the moment. I was wondering, is more polite, and I'd like to know is more direct.
As you may have noticed from the examples, it's necessary to make some grammatical changes
when asking indirect questions. In indirect questions, auxiliary verbs do, does, and did
are not used. So, don't say, could you tell me what time do the stores open? The correct
question is, could you tell me what time the stores open? Also, because the auxiliary verb
does is not used, we add s to verbs when the subject is singular. So, don't say, do you
know how does this machine work? The correct question is, do you know how this machine works?
Also, because the auxiliary verb did is not used, the verb is in the simple past for past
questions. If the direct question is, when did you send the documents, then the indirect
question is, I was wondering when you sent the documents. If the direct question is, how
much did you pay for the tickets? Then the indirect question is, could you tell me how
much you paid for the tickets? The next rule for indirect questions is that forms of the
verb to be, move from before to after the subject. So, don't say, I was wondering when was the
company founded? The correct question is, I was wondering when the company was founded.
Don't say, do you have any idea where are my keys? The correct way is, do you have any
idea where my keys are? If the direct question is a yes or no question, then the indirect
question will have the word if. For example, direct, does he like to ski? Indirect, do you
know if he likes to ski? Direct, did you have any trouble understanding the lecture? Indirect,
I was wondering if you had any trouble understanding the lecture. Finally, for present perfect questions,
we still use the auxiliary verbs have and has, but the position changes in indirect questions.
It goes from before to after the subject. Let's look at some examples. Direct, has the
client replied yet? Indirect, could you tell me if the client has replied yet? Direct, how
have your parents been? Indirect, I was wondering how your parents have been. These seem like a
lot of rules, but as you see and hear many examples of indirect questions, it'll get easier
to form them naturally. Finally, what do you say if someone asks you a question, but you
don't know the answer? Here are some phrases for saying you don't know. Sorry, I don't know.
I'm afraid I have no idea. I don't know, but I can find out. Say this when you are promising
to help discover the answer. I'm not sure, but I think. Say this, when you aren't certain
about the answer, but you'll try to guess. I have no clue. That's informal. Sorry, I can't
help you there. There are also a couple of rude ways to say you don't know the answer to a
question. For example, what are you asking me for? And, how the hell should I know? Those
phrases are used to express annoyance or anger that the person has asked you the question. They
should only be used if you're in a very bad mood and you want to be rude to the other person.
You finished lesson 31. Today's speaking task is to transform these direct questions into
indirect questions using the phrases in this lesson. It's okay to write out your answers
first, then record a message of yourself reading them aloud. Click the link in the lesson text
to record your message.
